item.title: How to leave WordPress without losing anything
item.description:
The short answer

Leaving WordPress is not moving files: it is keeping addresses, content and links while you change the machinery that publishes them. If the addresses are kept, rankings are kept. If they change without redirects, they are lost.

Why people leave

It is rarely ideology. It is usually one of three things:

  • Maintenance: weekly updates, plugins that break, nobody watching.
  • Speed: the site is slow because there is more machinery than needed.
  • Fear: fear that an update breaks the site, fear of attacks, fear of touching anything.

What is kept and what is lost

Kept: addresses (with parity and redirects), texts, images, files, publication dates and authorship where present.

item.title: Moving from WordPress to a static site
item.description:
Moving to a static site means no longer serving every visit with PHP and MySQL, and instead serving HTML files that are already built. The content is the same and so are the addresses, but the site loads faster, has a smaller attack surface and needs almost no maintenance.

When it makes sense

WordPress makes sense when many people edit, when there are orders and user accounts. When the site only publishes — news, projects, catalogues, portfolios — the machinery is surplus and turns into permanent maintenance work.

item.title: Konsento — Assembly Governance for Community Spaces
item.description:
Konsento is a free software web application that helps collectives, cooperatives and self-managed spaces make decisions in a transparent, structured and accessible way.

It was born from a real need: Nau Bostik, a self-managed cultural centre in the Sagrera neighbourhood of Barcelona, was managing its assemblies, working groups and agreements through instant messaging, scattered emails and unstructured shared documents. Decisions got lost, responsibilities became blurred and institutional memory disappeared with every change of people.

item.title: Cuida — Family care coordination app
item.description:
Cuida is a free, open-source web app built for families caring for a sick relative at home. It brings together everything you need to know: medical contacts, medication, emergency protocols and caregiver schedules — accessible from everyone’s phone.

It grew from a real need: coordinating a family of ten people around a grandfather with cardiorespiratory failure, continuous oxygen and morphine, supported by a palliative home care team (PADES). When you arrive at the emergency room at three in the morning, you can’t be searching for the GP’s name or which morphine dose he takes. Cuida has it all, one tap away.

item.title: Custom websites
item.description:
What “custom” means

It means the decisions come from the project: which pages are needed, how information is organised, how it reads on a phone and what the person editing it must be able to do. It does not mean “expensive” or “with more features”. It often means fewer things, done properly.

Most sites we see have the opposite problem: a template with twenty sections nobody fills, widgets that load for no known reason and an admin panel nobody understands. We start from a minimal base and add only what the project asks for.

item.title: Hugo or WordPress: which one fits you
item.description:
The short answer

Hugo if the site publishes information and you want few parts that can break. WordPress if you need a shop, users, a complex editorial workflow or an ecosystem of extensions that already covers your case.

The comparison, in one table

Criterion Hugo (static site) WordPress
Maintenance Almost none: no database Constant: core, plugins and backups
Speed Very high: pre-built files Depends on hosting and plugins
Attack surface Small: no admin panel Large: the most attacked target on the web
Editing Visual editor on text files Panel with menus and roles
Shop and users No (needs external services) Yes, built in
Extensions Few, and often not needed Thousands, with their maintenance
Bulk publishing Very good Very good
People who can work on it Fewer, but you never need to Many, and often you do

When Hugo fits you

  • Sites from 5 to 200 pages that inform about something: a cultural space, a band, a studio, a publisher, a restaurant.
  • Projects where nobody wants to think about updates.
  • Sites that must load fast on mobile and work in difficult conditions.
  • Projects where visitors’ data must not pass through third parties.

When WordPress fits you

  • A shop with stock, variants, coupons and shipping (WooCommerce).
  • A member area or courses with registrations and student tracking.
  • An editorial workflow with many roles, calendars and approvals.
  • When your team is already trained in WordPress and you just want to maintain it well.
  • When you depend on a very specific plugin that does exactly what you need.

What an agency selling WordPress will not tell you

That the real cost is not building the site: it is maintaining it. A site with fifteen plugins is monthly work someone must do — or nobody does. Many security and speed problems we see are not WordPress, they are that work not being paid for.

item.title: The new 112books.eu theme
item.description:
The problem wasn’t visual. It was structural.

112Books is an independent publisher based in Barcelona, specialising in photobooks and photographic projects. They guide photographers and authors through the entire process: layout, image selection and sequencing, printing, distribution.

Over the years, their website had grown without a clear plan. Content, sections and plugins kept being added. The result was a site that worked but didn’t explain clearly who 112Books is or what they do.

item.title: Web applications
item.description:
When a website is not enough

A website informs. An application does. The difference shows when the work has to be done every week and depends on someone who knows how: member lists, votes, bookings, time tracking, registrations, inventories, permissions.

If the process exists and lives on paper, in a spreadsheet only one person understands or in a group chat, there is an application to be built.

What we build

  • Association and collective management: members, dues, registrations, self-publishing of content.
  • Votes and decisions: anonymous voting, automatic counting, minutes and history.
  • Contests and juries: entries, works, public voting limited to the room and jury voting.
  • Time and jobs: hours per project, reports, invoicing from hours.
  • Content and publishing: platforms to publish with permissions and simple workflows.

When we do not build it

  • If a free tool already exists that does the job and can be adapted, we use it.
  • If the problem is communication, not software, we say so.
  • If the decision is to automate a process nobody has defined yet, we define it first.

How we do it

1. Understand the real process

We watch how the work is done now, on paper, in spreadsheets or in chat. The application must reproduce the process that works, not the one we wish existed.

item.title: Your WordPress is slow or got attacked: how to find out why
item.description:
The short answer

A slow or attacked WordPress almost never has a single cause. It is diagnosed by measuring three things: what the server sends, what the browser loads and what the admin area does. Without that data, “optimising” means changing things at random.

The usual causes, by frequency

  1. Overloaded shared hosting. The site is not slow: the neighbour is eating the machine.
  2. Plugins. Many, badly built or abandoned. Often there are fifteen and three are used.
  3. Bloated database. Revisions, transients, trash and old analytics tables.
  4. Unoptimised images. A 4 MB hero makes the site feel slow even when the server is fine.
  5. Automated attacks. Password guessing and mass requests to the admin area.
  6. Heavy theme. Page builders that load half a megabyte of code to show a headline.

How to diagnose it (without guessing)

  • Measure the server response time on a simple page.
  • Measure the weight and number of files on the homepage.
  • Check access logs: repeated attempts at wp-login or xmlrpc.
  • Check disk space and database health.
  • Review which plugins are active and which have never been updated.
  • Check certificate, backups and PHP version.

What to do depending on the result

  • Overloaded server → change hosting or hosting model.
  • Plugins → remove them, do not just deactivate.
  • Database → clean and limit revisions.
  • Images → convert and serve proper sizes.
  • Attacks → firewall, access limits and, if needed, take the admin panel off the internet.
  • All at once → maybe the question is not how to fix it, but whether this site should be a WordPress at all.

When the fix is not migrating

If the site sells, manages members or has a complex editorial workflow, changing technology fixes nothing: what exists needs care. Migrating is a solution for sites that only publish and demand more maintenance than they give back.

item.title: 9 Barris Imatge — from Blogger to Taro Photo App
item.description:
Where we started

The 9 Barris Imatge collective has been documenting the Nou Barris district of Barcelona since 2002. For years its whole archive lived on Blogger: 3,006 articles, the first ones from 2008, published by members who do photography, not IT.

Blogger was no longer enough. Every limitation turned into manual work for people who shouldn’t have to wrestle with a computer.

LinuxBCN’s answer wasn’t to switch platforms but to build one with free software: Taro Photo App, which combines a static website built with Hugo, a content manager so members can publish without touching code, and modules for audience voting and forms. The collective now owns both its data and its tools.

item.title: Audience vote — anonymous, in-person voting for exhibitions
item.description:
What it is

When an exhibition wants the audience to pick its favourite work, there are usually two options: a paper ballot box that’s hard to count, or an online form where anyone can vote from home as many times as they like.

This app does what neither manages: voting from your phone, only for people at the exhibition, one vote per work and person, with no personal data requested.

item.title: Taro Photo App — website, CMS and voting for photography collectives
item.description:
What it is

The 9 Barris Imatge collective has been documenting the Nou Barris district of Barcelona since 2002. Since 2018 it has published with its own system: Taro Photo App.

Taro has three parts, all free software:

  • A static website built with Hugo and the PaperMod theme, with a custom design.
  • A content manager (Sveltia CMS, hosted on the same site) so members can publish without touching code.
  • Python modules for what a static site can’t do alone: audience voting, forms that reach an inbox, and automatic publishing.

9barrisimatge.org is the reference installation: 3,008 articles, 24 member profiles and 19 years of archive. The distributed software is the same system without the collective’s data, so any other photography group can install it with its own members, articles and albums.

item.title: Blog de Pocallum — From Blogger to WordPress, from WordPress to Hugo
item.description:
Goodbye WordPress, hello Hugo

The Blog de Pocallum —a photographic chronicle of concerts, festivals, cameras and neighbourhood life in Barcelona since 2010— has switched engines entirely, and it’s not the first time. The result of this latest step: more speed, less attack surface, and the exact same content at the exact same URLs.

Three eras, one blog

The blog hasn’t always lived on WordPress. It started on Blogger, Google’s free platform: convenient to get going, but with content, data and design under a third party’s control, with neither sovereignty nor long-term predictability.

item.title: Terra i Foc: Catalan artisanal ceramics, now online
item.description:
From LinuxBCN.com we have just published the new website of Terra i Foc, the artisanal ceramics workshop founded in 1969 by Joan Martínez Peidro and Isabel Serres in the Penedès region. A history of over fifty years of clay, fire and hands that now has a place to tell itself to the world.

What we built

A bilingual site (Catalan and English) that gathers the memory of the workshop in five main sections:

item.title: LinuxBCN Analytics for GoatCounter
item.description:
The problem with Google Analytics

Most websites use Google Analytics. It’s free, powerful, and has been the standard for years. But it has a hidden cost: it requires a cookie consent banner, it sends data to Google’s servers, and it puts your traffic data in the hands of an advertising platform.

For many projects — blogs, artist websites, independent publishers, small businesses — Google Analytics is overkill. What they need is to know how many visits they’re getting, which pages perform best, and where visitors come from. Nothing more.

item.title: Ressona — Digital Identity for Artists
item.description:
When image and technology speak the same language

Ressona was born from the convergence of two trajectories: Pocallum, with years of accompanying artists in photography and visual identity, and LinuxBCN, building web infrastructure with free software. The result is a brand designed for musicians, actors, dancers, visual artists and emerging creators who need a solid digital presence without sacrificing coherence.

The name comes from ressonar (to resonate): to echo, to vibrate. A digital identity should do exactly that — amplify what the artist already is.

item.title: Pocallum — Cultural Photography with a Renewed Digital Presence
item.description:
Joan Linux Martínez has been photographing jazz, blues, theatre, flamenco and performing arts in Barcelona since 2010. For years, his website lived on WordPress. In 2026, we migrated everything to Hugo and GitHub Pages. This is what we built and why.

The project

pocallum.cat is the professional website of Pocallum, a cultural photography service specialising in live music, theatre and dance. The site brings together 152 photographs, 27 festivals, 11 news articles, services and contact pages, static internal search and a custom analytics dashboard. All of it in Catalan and English.

item.title: Estenop — Pinhole calculator
item.description:
The physics, solved on your phone

A pinhole camera has no lens. Just a hole. And that hole dictates everything: the light that enters, the time required, the light captured on film.

The problem is that pinhole physics leaves no room for calculation errors. An effective aperture of f/128 or f/180, combined with the reciprocity characteristics of each emulsion, produces numbers that are hard to work out in your head. Until now.

item.title: Hosting and maintenance
item.description:
What maintenance includes

  • Hosting on our own server, with HTTPS and certificates up to date.
  • Backups daily, outside the hosting server and rotated.
  • Monitoring of availability, certificate and domain.
  • Planned updates for whatever needs them, tested first.
  • Support for small changes: a paragraph, an image, a new section.
  • Periodic review of broken links, accessibility and performance.

Why “install and forget” is not enough

A static site has very few moving parts, and that is already an advantage: no database or plugins that must be updated every week. But it still depends on things it does not control: a certificate that expires, a domain that lapses, the server it lives on, an image someone deletes or a link that stops working.

item.title: Moving from Blogger to your own site
item.description:
The short answer

Leaving Blogger is mostly about taking the content out of Google’s cloud: posts, images and comments. Addresses are kept, but images must be downloaded and hosted on your own infrastructure, because today they live on Google servers.

Why people leave

  • Control: content sits on a platform that decides for you (design, templates, features).
  • Speed and looks: Blogger templates are far behind what can be done today.
  • Trust: platforms that shut services or change terms. It has happened before.
  • Sovereignty: photos, texts and comments are yours, but you do not hold them.

What to preserve

  • The posts, with date, author and tags.
  • The images, which today point at Google servers.
  • The addresses of each post and each tag.
  • The comments, if you want to keep them.
  • The domain, which is what makes nothing change place.

The 9 Barris Imatge case

A photography collective in Nou Barris has documented the neighbourhood since 2002, and since 2008 published it on Blogger. 3,006 posts written by people who do photography, not IT.

item.title: Ivan Kovačević
item.description:
One musician, many projects, one website

Ivan Kovačević is a Serbian double bassist based in Barcelona since 2001. He has played with Los Mambo Jambo, The Nu Niles and Down Home, is a founding member of the Barcelona Gipsy balKan Orchestra, leads the Barcelona Big Blues Band and fronts Bratia. He has played on more than fifty records.

His website had gone through iWeb and then WordPress. Neither solved the real problem: how to present a career spread across many bands without the site turning into a messy drawer.

item.title: Positivitzador WebApp
item.description:
Llumàtics.com chemical photography training

Some tools make noise. Others simply solve things.

Positivitzador was born from a very specific need: understanding what you’re looking at when working with negatives. No gimmicks, no pointless filters. Open the camera, look… and see the image as a positive.

Designed for darkrooms, workshops, and photochemical processes, this small web app does one thing —and does it well—: invert the image in real time so you can read light, contrast, and composition with clarity.

item.title: What a band's website needs to cover
item.description:
The short answer

A band’s website is not a shop window: it is the place where someone who does not know you decides whether to listen to you, book you or move on. They do it in a few seconds with four questions: who you are, what you sound like, when you play and how to book you. If the site answers them without making people think, the rest is decoration.

item.title: Analytics and GDPR
item.description:
Analytics that do not spy

Most analytics tools do not measure the site: they build a profile of every visitor and sell it or keep it for other uses. We do the opposite: we count visits, pages and sources without identifying people, with our own counter on the same domain that cannot be blocked and needs no cookies.

What we measure and what we do not

Yes: visits, most-viewed pages, language, device, aggregated source and conversions (for example, how many people submit the form).

item.title: Barcelona Big Blues Band
item.description:
Europe’s largest rhythm & blues big band

The Barcelona Big Blues Band is an ensemble of up to fifteen musicians led by double bassist Ivan Kovačević, based at Barcelona’s Jamboree Jazz Club for more than ten years. It plays blues, swing and rhythm & blues in big-band format and backs guest artists such as Dani Nel·lo, Ray Gelato, Mike Sanchez and Myriam Swanson.

The previous site was a WordPress install: plugins for everything, even for the cookie banner, and a structure that didn’t match what a band needs to show.

item.title: Time Tracker
item.description:
The idea

The trouble with traditional time-tracking tools is that you have to remember to start and stop them.

So we turned it around: if we already use Claude Code for almost everything, why not build time tracking into the assistant itself? When a session opens, the tracker starts. When it closes, the time is logged. Every request made during the session is recorded as a subtask. All automatic. All in local Markdown files, with no subscriptions and no external services.

item.title: Bratia
item.description:
Balkan Gypsy Jazz from Barcelona

Bratia is a Barcelona band formed by musicians with international careers — Ivan Kovačević, Pere Nolasc Plana, Victor Paradis, Julien Chanal and Stelios Togias — specialising in the fusion of manouche jazz, Balkan music and gypsy jazz.

The previous website was a heavy, hard-to-maintain WordPress that required technical intervention for any change. The real problem: touring musicians don’t have time to manage websites.

The problem

An active band needs the website to update itself.

item.title: Machiroku
item.description:
A Japanese restaurant in the heart of Barcelona

Machiroku is a small family restaurant specialising in authentic Japanese cuisine in the heart of Barcelona.

The previous website was a conventional WordPress: functional, but heavy, hard to maintain and with no adaptation to the restaurant’s real needs.

The problem

A restaurant needs to update its menu, opening hours and notices frequently. With WordPress, every change required accessing a complex manager or depending on someone external.

item.title: Nau Bostik
item.description:
A project in two phases

Nau Bostik is a self-managed sociocultural space in the Sagrera neighbourhood, Barcelona. Intense activity, diverse community, constant agenda and completely horizontal management.

Our relationship with the project has had two distinct stages.

Phase 1 — Emergency recovery

When the old website stopped working, the situation needed an immediate response. We built a functional, stable and clean site in the shortest possible time: enough to maintain the space’s digital presence while the real solution was being prepared.

item.title: Llumàtics
item.description:
From WordPress to Hugo: a site that grows with the project

In 2020, Llumàtics launched with a standard WordPress setup. It worked, but each season the project demanded more: new sections, documentation for students, integration between the schedule and courses, faster load times… The general-purpose CMS had become a bottleneck.

In 2026 we migrated to a site built from scratch with Hugo: multilingual architecture, high performance, and a structure designed specifically for an analogue photography school.

item.title: 112Books
item.description:
A publisher that accompanies authors

112Books is an independent publisher in Barcelona specialising in photobooks and photographic projects. It does more than print: it accompanies photographers and authors through the whole process — from the first idea to the finished work — with layout, image selection and sequencing, printing, print runs and distribution.

It is a LinuxBCN project of our own, which is also why we use it as a test bed: if we would not trust a decision for a client, we do not make it here either.

item.title: 112 Revelats
item.description:
A platform for new voices in photography

112 Revelats is a project by publisher 112Books to give visibility to emerging photographers through the collective photobook format.

Two open calls per year. Each edition, a group of authors publishes a digital photobook together. If the project takes root, also in print.

The website has migrated from WordPress to Hugo — lighter, faster and fully self-managed via Git.

Tech stack

Hugo extended — native Sass processing, no runtime dependencies.
GitHub Pages — global CDN, automatic deploy.
GitHub Actions — automated build and deploy in ~20 seconds.
GoatCounter — cookieless analytics, GDPR-compliant, with custom dashboard.
Formspree — submission forms without proprietary backend.

item.title: 40 Years of Blues in Barcelona
item.description:
A living archive for a paper archive

On November 6, 2026, the book 40 Years of Blues in Barcelona by Joan Linux with texts by Manuel López Poy was presented at Centre Cultural Collblanc – La Torrassa.

Commissioned by 112books.eu — the photography publisher that Joan Linux runs.

The accompanying website is not merely a book listing: it is a living photographic and biographical archive of Barcelona’s blues scene.

The challenge

Organise 148 musician profiles, 531 formations and 296 black-and-white photographs across three languages. Without a content management system. Without unnecessary external dependencies. So anyone can search for a musician, see their face, understand why Barcelona is a blues city, and navigate connections: which other musician plays the same instrument, which bands share members, which musicians played together over the years.

item.title: MalditasMaquinas
item.description:
Technology consultancy by the hour

MalditasMaquinas is an on-demand technology consultancy service for artists, freelancers and small businesses. A merger of two brands with over 20 years of history: MalditasMaquinas.com and MacBCN.com.

The model is simple and clean: clients buy a prepaid block of hours and submit technical queries by email from their private area. No hours, no support. No subscriptions, no monthly commitments.

Distributed and secure backend

All business logic runs on Cloudflare Workers — no central server, no single point of failure. The database is D1 (SQLite distributed across Cloudflare’s global network), sessions are handled with KV, and consultation attachments are stored in R2. Authentication uses magic links with JWT in an HttpOnly cookie — no passwords, no leaks.

item.title: A.W.P.C.P.
item.description:
14 editions of Worldwide Pinhole Photography Day in Barcelona

A.W.P.C.P. organises the Worldwide Pinhole Photography Day in Barcelona since 2011. Every last Sunday of April, photographers around the world shoot a pinhole camera at the same moment. Barcelona has participated since the first edition.

The website had been running on a WordPress server with fourteen years of accumulated content. In 2024 we migrated it to Hugo + GitHub Pages: no server, no database, all content versioned in Git.

item.title: Carrer.cat
item.description:
The neighbourhood movement’s magazine, online

Carrer is the publication of the FAVB —Federation of Neighbourhood Associations of Barcelona— with decades of work defending neighbourhood rights. It is a magazine made by people from the neighbourhoods, describing the city from the ground up: housing, mobility, public space, social rights.

The challenge was to bring a consolidated print publication online without losing its editorial essence.

A website of its own, separated from the federation

The magazine used to live inside the FAVB website. We split it off because they are two different things: a federation that coordinates, informs and serves its associations, and a publication with its own rhythm, structure and image.

item.title: FAVB
item.description:
A federation with decades of history

The FAVB —Federation of Neighbourhood Associations of Barcelona— is one of the oldest and most representative neighbourhood organisations in the city. It brings together neighbourhood associations, coordinates campaigns and publishes its own content.

For an organisation like this the website is not a business card: it is infrastructure. Publications, announcements, documents and campaigns that the city reads pass through it.

Years administering this website

We have been administering the FAVB website for years. In that time it has been through many phases: template changes, new sections, moves, emergency patches and clean-ups. This is the kind of site that is not built in a day: it is maintained.

item.title: Pocallum
item.description:
Cultural photography with its own character

Pocallum is Joan Linux Martínez’s photography service: live music, theatre, dance and the performing arts in Barcelona, since 2010. An author’s craft, with a very defined visual identity and an unconventional way of working.

The site had to do one very specific thing: make anyone looking for a photographer for a concert or a show understand in ten seconds whose eye they are dealing with.

item.title: LinuxBCN.com
item.description:
Our own website as a first project

If we recommend a way of working, the least we can do is apply it to ourselves.

LinuxBCN.com is the project where we have implemented, tested and refined every technical decision we later bring to clients: lightweight architecture, privacy by design, real accessibility and data sovereignty. It’s not an artificial example — it’s the system we use every day.

The problem

The previous website was a WordPress. Functional, but:

item.title: GoatCounter Dashboard
item.description:
Clear analytics for static websites

A web analytics dashboard that shows exactly what you need to know about your visitors. No noise. No cookies. No subscriptions.

The problem

Conventional analytics tools — Google Analytics and similar — are built for marketing teams that want aggressive tracking. For a local business, a school or an association, they’re excessive, invasive, and often blocked by browsers.

GoatCounter is a free, privacy-respecting alternative. But its interface isn’t immediate: you have to interpret tables, navigate through panels, and the workflow is slow and manual.

item.title: Family Art Tattoo
item.description:
A tattoo studio with a different way of communicating

Family Art Tattoo is a tattoo studio in Barcelona with a clear philosophy: accompanying the client through the entire body decoration process, from first contact to aftercare.

This way of understanding the service needed a digital presence that expressed it. Not a photo catalogue, but a real communication tool.

What we did

Custom WordPress theme, built from scratch

Designed and developed entirely to specification, with a dark and expressive aesthetic coherent with the world of tattooing. No purchased templates, no third-party visual frameworks. The design was born from the project, not the other way around.

item.title: 9 Barris Acull
item.description:
A necessary organisation

For years, 9 Barris Acull was one of the reference organisations for the reception and support of newcomers in the Nou Barris district of Barcelona. Hundreds of cases annually, thousands of accumulated users, and a solid track record of rigorous, necessary social work.

The withdrawal of public funding forced its closure.

We keep the website open as a testimony to work well done.

What we did

The WordPress design was not our work, but many of the communication strategies were — and above all, the most important tool in the project: a web application developed with Drupal that centralised all of the organisation’s internal management.

item.title: Solutions for artists and musicians
item.description:
The usual situation

You have a website, social media, content — but no system.

Concerts not updated. Biography different on every platform. Videos on YouTube, photos on Instagram, music on Spotify, and the website connects none of it.

Any change requires touching five different places. Or depending on someone else to do it.

What we propose

A digital presence designed as a system.

A website that connects what already exists — concerts, music, videos, photographs — without duplicating content or creating new dependencies.

item.title: Solutions for cultural entities and collectives
item.description:
The usual situation

The collective works. The digital communication doesn’t.

The website is hard to update — it always depends on someone. Meetings are called via WhatsApp. Documents live on Google Drive without anyone having decided that. Photos are on someone’s Instagram who may no longer be in the collective.

It’s not bad will. It’s that nobody designed the system.

What we propose

Organising the collective’s digital ecosystem with criteria.

item.title: Solutions for values-driven businesses
item.description:
The usual situation

The business works. The digital presence doesn’t quite work.

The website was made by someone years ago and nobody knows how to touch it. You’re on Instagram because “you have to be” but it generates nothing. You pay subscriptions to tools you don’t remember why you signed up for. Every update requires calling someone or waiting until they have time.

The problem isn’t the technology. It’s that nobody thought the system through from the start.
